title: The 365 days
text: Six study days, then a lighter seventh, fifty-two times over, then the capstone. Every seventh day is a Thursday and is deliberately unallocated. Eleven of those seventh days are milestones instead, where the week’s work turns into something you could show someone.

title: Milestones
text:
Days pass and leave nothing behind unless you write something down. These twelve are what the year is actually for; the other three hundred and fifty-three days feed them.
Each milestone replaces that week’s catch-up day. The work happens during the week. The milestone day is where it becomes a document — which means if the week went badly, the milestone tells you so, and that is the point.
A note on what “good” means here. Every milestone below has a How you know it’s good line, and in almost every case it is a line about honesty rather than performance. A milestone that reports a Sharpe of 3.1 and cannot say how many strategies were tried before that one is a worse artifact than one reporting 0.6 with a confidence interval. Interviewers at the firms you are targeting can tell the difference in about ninety seconds, and so can you.

title: Milestones
section: Milestone 1 — Market map and a point-in-time data store
text:
Milestone 1 — Market map and a point-in-time data store
Day 28, Thursday 3 September 2026. Fed by weeks 1–4.
Two things: a written map of the industry, and working code that stores prices without lying about what was knowable when.
What’s in it

A one-page map of who pays whom: exchanges, brokers, clearing, market makers, prop shops, pod shops, long-only managers, allocators. For each, where the revenue comes from. This exists so that eleven months from now you can tell which firm you are actually interviewing at.
A glossary in your own words of every instrument you met — share, ETF, future, option, bond, forward — written as “what this contract obliges each side to do”, not as a definition you copied.
A DuckDB or Parquet store of daily bars for a universe you chose and can defend, with splits and dividends handled explicitly, and a documented answer to “what did this series look like on 12 March 2019, using only information available on 12 March 2019”.
The ingestion re-runs from scratch with one command.

How you know it’s good — you can state what your data source does not contain (delisted names? restated fundamentals? the actual close or the auction print?) without going to look.

title: Milestones
section: Milestone 2 — Stylized facts and the noise floor
text:
Milestone 2 — Stylized facts and the noise floor
Day 63, Thursday 8 October 2026. Fed by weeks 5–9.
The document you will reread every time a backtest looks good. Half empirical, half simulation.
What’s in it

The stylized facts, measured on your own data rather than quoted: the return distribution against a fitted normal, an estimated tail index, the autocorrelation of returns next to the autocorrelation of absolute returns, and the leverage effect.
The Sharpe ratio treated as an estimator. Its standard error at your sample length. What serial correlation does to it. How long a track record has to be before a Sharpe of 1 is distinguishable from 0 at any confidence you would act on.
The noise floor: a simulation that answers, for your own research process, how high a backtested Sharpe must be before it is evidence of anything, given the number of specifications you will try. Deflated Sharpe, and the probability of backtest overfitting, computed rather than cited.
One paragraph mapping each of the above onto the equivalent problem in genome-wide association studies, because that mapping is the thing you will say in an interview that nobody else says.

How you know it’s good — it produces a specific number that you are willing to be held to for the rest of the year, and you actually apply it in milestone 3.

title: Milestones
section: Milestone 3 — A pairs strategy that survives out of sample
text:
Milestone 3 — A pairs strategy that survives out of sample
Day 98, Thursday 12 November 2026. Fed by weeks 10–14.
The first end-to-end strategy. Deliberately the most-published, most-degraded idea in the field, so that the exercise is about method rather than about finding an edge.
What’s in it

The pair selection procedure, stated before the results, including how many pairs were screened. That count feeds directly into milestone 2’s correction.
Cointegration tested properly — Engle-Granger and Johansen, with the difference explained — plus the estimated half-life of mean reversion and the trading rule derived from it rather than tuned onto it.
A hedge ratio that is allowed to move, via the Kalman filter from week 14, compared against a static one.
Out-of-sample results on a period you did not look at while developing, with costs, and the same procedure run on synthetic independent random walks to show the false-positive rate of your own pipeline.

How you know it’s good — you can say what would have made you abandon it, and whether that condition was met. If the honest answer is “it doesn’t work after costs”, the milestone is complete and successful.

title: Milestones
section: Milestone 4 — A factor risk model built from scratch
text:
Milestone 4 — A factor risk model built from scratch
Day 133, Thursday 17 December 2026. Fed by weeks 15–19.
Not a call to a library. The covariance matrix, the factor exposures, and the decomposition, built by you.
What’s in it

A covariance matrix over a few hundred names, estimated three ways — sample, Ledoit-Wolf shrunk, and factor-based — with the eigenvalue spectrum plotted against the Marchenko-Pastur bound so it is visible which eigenvalues carry information.
Factor exposures for market, size, value and momentum, and a decomposition of one portfolio’s risk into factor and idiosyncratic parts.
The same portfolio optimized under each covariance estimate, and the out-of-sample realized risk of each, against equal weighting as the benchmark.
A position-sizing section: what full Kelly implies, what fraction of it you would actually run, and the drawdown you are accepting by choosing that fraction.

How you know it’s good — equal weighting appears in the comparison and is not quietly excluded when it wins.

title: Milestones
text:
Milestone 5 — The research platform
Day 161, Thursday 14 January 2027. Fed by weeks 20–23.
The single most valuable artifact of the year, and the one an interviewer will ask the most questions about. Everything after this is built on it.
What’s in it

An event-driven backtester that consumes point-in-time data, applies a documented cost model, and produces a standard result object.
A transaction cost model with the components separated — spread, impact, borrow, financing — and a chart of net Sharpe against turnover, so the strategy’s sensitivity to costs is visible rather than assumed.
A test suite whose job is to make look-ahead impossible rather than unlikely. At minimum: a test that feeds the engine data with future values deliberately poisoned and asserts the results are unchanged; a test on synthetic data with an analytically known answer; and a null-strategy test whose distribution of outcomes you have characterised.
A written list of every lie your backtester still tells, ranked by how much it matters. There will be several. This list is the most impressive part of the document.

How you know it’s good — someone else could clone it, run one command, and reproduce a result you report elsewhere in the year.

title: Milestones
text:
Milestone 6 — The alpha book
Day 203, Thursday 25 February 2027. Fed by weeks 24–29.
Five to eight signals, each characterised the way a research desk characterises one.
What’s in it

Per signal: the economic reason it might work stated first, then information coefficient and its decay profile, information ratio, quantile spread, turnover, and estimated capacity in dollars.
The correlation matrix of the signals, and the combination — with the argument for why you combined the way you did rather than the way that scored best.
At least one signal that does not work, kept in the book with the diagnosis.
Everything run through the milestone-5 platform, with the multiple-testing correction from milestone 2 applied to the whole set rather than to each signal in isolation.

How you know it’s good — the number of specifications you tried is stated on the first page.

title: Milestones
section: Milestone 7 — Machine learning against the linear baseline
text:
Milestone 7 — Machine learning against the linear baseline
Day 238, Thursday 1 April 2027. Fed by weeks 30–34.
The report that decides whether the machine learning earned its complexity. Given your background this is the milestone you are most at risk of doing well and concluding too much from.
What’s in it

The labelling scheme and why — fixed horizon against triple barrier — and the sample weights that overlapping outcomes force on you.
Purged, embargoed cross-validation, with the embargo length justified from the autocorrelation of the labels rather than picked.
A regularized linear model as the baseline, taken seriously and tuned as carefully as the gradient boosting. Most published comparisons lose here by not trying.
The verdict on the same test set with the same costs, plus a permutation-importance analysis and an honest note on which features are proxies for something you did not intend.

How you know it’s good — the conclusion is a number with an interval, and you would report it the same way if it had come out the other direction.

title: Milestones
section: Milestone 8 — An option pricer and a delta-hedging study
text:
Milestone 8 — An option pricer and a delta-hedging study
Day 280, Thursday 13 May 2027. Fed by weeks 35–40.
Two artifacts: code that prices, and a simulation that shows what hedging actually earns.
What’s in it

A pricer implementing Black-Scholes analytically, a binomial tree, and Monte Carlo with at least one variance-reduction technique — all three agreeing to a stated tolerance, with the convergence of the last two plotted against the first.
The greeks, computed analytically and by finite difference, agreeing.
The delta-hedging study: simulate hedging a short option at some volatility while the underlying realizes another, and decompose the profit and loss. Show that the expected result is the gap between implied and realized variance, and show what discrete rebalancing costs you.
A page on the variance risk premium: what it is, what the historical evidence says about its size, and why it is not free money.

How you know it’s good — you can derive Black-Scholes on a whiteboard by the replication argument, without notes, in ten minutes. Test yourself on this rather than assuming.

title: Milestones
section: Milestone 9 — Execution, impact and honest capacity
text:
Milestone 9 — Execution, impact and honest capacity
Day 308, Thursday 10 June 2027. Fed by weeks 41–44.
The milestone that revises every earlier number downward. Expect that and report it plainly.
What’s in it

An impact model fitted to real intraday or order-book data, with the square-root form tested rather than assumed, and the fitted coefficient stated with its uncertainty.
Your own slippage, measured against arrival price on the paper account, split into spread, impact and timing.
The revised capacity of the milestone-6 alpha book once that impact model replaces the flat cost assumption, at several assumed asset levels.
One paragraph on which of your strategies dies first as size grows, and why.

How you know it’s good — it contains at least one earlier result that you now believe was wrong, said in those words.

title: Milestones
text:
Milestone 10 — The system in production
Day 329, Thursday 1 July 2027. Fed by weeks 45–47.
The strategy running by itself, against a real broker’s paper account, without you.
What’s in it

Scheduled execution: data pull, signal computation, portfolio construction, order generation, submission, and reconciliation, each logged and each able to fail loudly.
Monitoring that catches the failures that matter — stale data, a position that does not match the intended one, a fill far from the expected price, a signal outside its historical range.
The reconciliation report: intended portfolio against actual portfolio, daily, with the difference explained.
A runbook for the four or five things that will go wrong, written before they do.

How you know it’s good — it survives a week where you do not touch it, and the log tells you what happened without you having to reconstruct it.

title: Milestones
text:
Milestone 11 — The interview dossier
Day 357, Thursday 29 July 2027. Fed by weeks 48–51 and by fifty drill sittings.
Everything a hiring process needs from you, assembled and rehearsed.
What’s in it

A CV rewritten for this industry, where the genetics work is described in the language of the job you want — instrumental variables, multiple testing, high-dimensional inference — without overclaiming or disowning it.
Two-page write-ups of milestones 5, 6 and 8, each readable by someone with ten minutes.
The problem log from the drill thread: what you have solved, what you got wrong, and the classes of problem you are still slow on.
The five-minute research presentation, rehearsed against a clock and recorded once so you have heard it.
The firm list with a reason next to each name, and the outreach actually sent.

How you know it’s good — you can answer “why are you leaving academia” in three sentences that a researcher at the firm would find convincing rather than polite.

title: Milestones
text:
Milestone 12 — Capstone
Day 365, Friday 6 August 2027.
Three things.
The research dossier pulls the year into one document: the platform, the alpha book, the risk model, the execution study, and the recommendation you would give a portfolio manager about which of it is worth running and at what size.
The track record is whatever the paper account did, reported without adjustment. Months where it lost money are in the table. If the live period disagrees with the backtest, that disagreement is the most interesting result you have and it goes at the front.
The retrospective is the page you will value most in 2029: what you believed in September 2026 that turned out to be wrong, what took three times longer than planned, which milestone you would drop, and what you would do differently with the next 365 hours. Answer the self-check out loud first — anything you cannot answer is not a failure, it is the reading list for the autumn.

title: Hiring
text:
This page exists because a study plan that does not say what it is aiming at is a hobby. Everything here is about the thing the other 365 pages are for: a seat as a buy-side quantitative researcher, applied for during 2027.
The last section is the uncomfortable one and it is the reason to read this in September rather than in June, because two of the gaps take a year to close and one of them you close by choosing differently.

title: Hiring
section: The seat you are aiming at
text:
The seat you are aiming at
Quantitative researcher, systematic equity or multi-asset. You are given data, a research platform and a mandate, and you produce signals that go into a book someone else risks capital on. The work is statistics under adversarial conditions: the effects are small, the data is non-stationary, most of what you find is not real, and the cost of being wrong is measured rather than argued about.
That description is not a coincidence. It is the seat where your existing training transfers hardest, and the mapping is specific:







What you do now
What it is called there




Mendelian randomization
Instrumental variable estimation


Genome-wide significance, winner’s curse
Backtest overfitting, the deflated Sharpe ratio


Colocalization
Bayesian model comparison over shared-signal hypotheses


Conditioning an LD matrix
Shrinking a return covariance matrix


Not splitting relatives across folds
Purged, embargoed cross-validation


Ascertainment bias in a cohort
Survivorship bias in a universe



Four adjacent seats you will see advertised, and how they differ:

Quantitative trader. Faster horizons, more decisions per day, and the interview is a trading game rather than a research presentation. Weeks 41–44 and 49 are the parts of this course that point here.
Quantitative developer. Building the platform rather than the signals. Better paid at the entry level, harder to move out of into research than people expect. Phase 10 is the relevant preparation and it is not enough on its own.
Quantitative analyst, sell side. Derivatives pricing and risk at a bank. More mathematics, less data, much less of your existing training used. Phase 8 is the relevant preparation.
Data scientist at a systematic manager. Sometimes the same job with a different title and sometimes a support function. Ask, in the first call, whose profit and loss the work appears in.

title: Hiring
section: Who hires, and what the structure does to the job
text:
Who hires, and what the structure does to the job
Four structures, and the difference matters more than the brand:
Multi-manager pod shops — Millennium, Point72, Balyasny, Citadel’s equities business. A portfolio manager runs a book, you are on their team, and the drawdown limit is real and short. Fastest entry, fastest exit, and the highest variance in outcome. Ask what happens to the team if the book is down 5 percent.
Partnerships and prop firms — Jane Street, Optiver, IMC, SIG, Hudson River. Trade their own capital, no external investors, longer horizons on people. The bar at entry is the highest and the interview is the most standardised, which is good for you because a standardised process rewards preparation.
Systematic managers — AQR, Man AHL, Winton, Two Sigma, D. E. Shaw. Research at longer horizons, published papers, closest to what you have spent this year doing and the closest cultural match to academia. Slowest hiring, smallest number of seats.
Bank quant groups. Different work, mentioned for completeness. Better hours, lower ceiling.

title: Hiring
text:
The process, round by round
Roughly five stages over four to eight weeks, and each one is testing something different:

Screen. CV against a filter, human or otherwise. This is where the genetics background is either a differentiator or a reason to stop reading, and which one it is depends entirely on the vocabulary on the first page. Day 351 is about that.
Online test. Timed probability and mathematics, often an hour, often unforgiving. This round has no partial credit and no conversation, and it is the one the drill thread exists for. Fifty sittings of twenty minutes is the preparation; four weeks in July is not.
Technical phone screens. One to three of them. Probability out loud, statistics, coding, and for a research seat a conversation about something you built. The failure mode here is length, not correctness — week 50 is entirely about compressing correct answers into ninety seconds.
The superday. Four to six back-to-back rounds: probability under a clock, a trading or estimation game, a coding round, your research presentation, and one behavioural conversation. Nobody tells you which is next. Day 355 exists because the transitions are what actually degrade.
Offer and negotiation. Day 356. The short version: the sign-on and any first-year guarantee move, the base moves within a band, the deferral schedule does not, and the leverage comes entirely from having a second process finishing at the same time.

What each round is really testing. The probability rounds test whether you can be quantitative under time pressure with someone watching, which is a different skill from being quantitative. The research presentation tests whether you know which of your results is weakest. The trading game tests whether you update on evidence when the evidence is that someone chose to trade with you. None of these are tests of what you know.

title: Hiring
text:
Timing

Autumn 2026 through spring 2027 — no applications. You have nothing to show yet and a rejection now costs you the same firm later.
March–April 2027 — the firm list and the outreach for conversations rather than roles (day 353, day 354). Referrals take months to become anything and this is the last point at which starting them still works.
May–July 2027 — applications, in a batch rather than sequentially. Batching is what gives you two offers in the same fortnight, and two offers in the same fortnight is the only real negotiating position that exists.
August–October 2027 — processes run. Expect four to eight weeks each and expect several to end without explanation.

Two calendar facts worth knowing: the campus pipelines these firms run for graduating PhDs fill in the autumn for the following summer, and you are not in that pipeline. Experienced-hire processes run continuously and are less predictable but also less seasonal, which is the route you are on.

title: Hiring
text:
The honest gaps
You are a career changer, and the default pipeline is not built for you. The standard hire is a PhD in physics, mathematics or computer science, recruited in their final year through a campus process, with no industry experience and no expectation of any. You are a postdoc in a different field applying laterally. That is not disqualifying and it does mean every application is a non-standard one, which raises the value of a referral from a low multiple to the single largest factor in the outcome.
You have no track record anyone can verify. A paper-traded year is not a track record and will not be treated as one. What it is is evidence of process, which is a different and still useful thing. The two public records that carry actual weight are a Numerai history with real submissions over time (day 230) and a placing in a serious competition. Both take months of elapsed time, which is why they are in the course early rather than in phase 11.
Madison is not where these jobs are. They are in New York, Chicago, London, and a small number in the Bay Area, Amsterdam and Hong Kong. Remote research seats exist and are rare and mostly go to people with an existing track record at the firm. Decide before you apply whether you will move, because the answer changes the firm list and it is a question you will be asked in the first call.
The competition is specifically good at the interview. The pool includes people who have been doing timed competitive mathematics since they were sixteen and who will beat you on the online test on speed alone. The drill thread is the only response to that and it works by accumulating fifty sittings rather than by intensity.
Your background reads as biology to a screener. This is the gap you close cheapest and it is entirely a vocabulary problem. “Genome-wide association study of protein levels” and “high-dimensional multiple testing with a controlled error rate across 10 million correlated hypotheses” describe the same work, and only one of them survives a thirty-second CV scan by someone hiring for statistical arbitrage.
You will not be a C++ programmer in a year. Phase 10 gets you to reading a matching engine and writing something small that works. That is a real and defensible claim and it is not the same as the claim a low-latency firm needs. It closes the quantitative developer route and closes most of high-frequency trading, and both of those were closed anyway for reasons that have nothing to do with C++.
The base rate is against any individual application, and that is the wrong frame. The relevant questions are how many processes you can run in parallel, how many are warm rather than cold, and whether what you can show is different from what everyone else shows. You control all three. Nobody applying from a physics PhD arrives with instrumental variables and massive multiple testing already in their hands, and that is the entire argument for this year.
One year at an hour a day is not a PhD in this field. By August 2027 you will be able to hold a research conversation, build a defensible backtest, derive Black-Scholes and pass a probability round. There are people three years into the seat you want who have forgotten more market structure than this course covers. The plan is to be hireable, not to be finished.

title: Hiring
text:
What actually changes the outcome
In rough order of effect:

A referral. One warm introduction is worth more than twenty applications, and warm introductions come from conversations started months earlier about something specific the person worked on.
A work product someone can read in ten minutes. The three two-page write-ups from milestone 11. Almost nobody applying has one, and it converts a screening decision from a guess into a reading.
The drill thread, finished. Not started in June. The online test has no partial credit and the probability round is the most common single point of failure for exactly the kind of candidate you are.
Being able to say what is weakest in your own work. Milestone 9 requires you to name an earlier result you now believe was wrong. That habit is the most distinguishing thing you can bring into a research conversation, and it is rarer than it should be.

title: Hiring
section: If it does not work in 2027
text:
If it does not work in 2027
Three outcomes that are not failure, listed because deciding in advance which of them you would accept stops the decision being made under pressure in November:

An adjacent seat with a path. A quantitative developer or data science role at a systematic manager, moving into research from inside. Slower, and internal moves have a much higher success rate than external applications.
Applying again in 2028 with a live track record. A second year of the paper account, or a real one, plus a Numerai history with two years of submissions, is a materially different application from the 2027 one.
Running your own capital and not changing jobs. Everything in this course works at small size, and the strategies with capacity too small for a fund to bother with are the ones you can actually run. The capstone asks what you would run with your own money and at what size, and a serious answer to that question is worth having regardless of what happens to the applications.

 30 min Explain your measurement: a cache line brings in 64 bytes, so iterating over one field of a struct array wastes most of every line, while a columnar layout uses all of it.  20 min Connect it back: Parquet is struct-of-arrays on disk for the same reason, and your day 311 measurement of bytes read is the same effect one level up the hierarchy. Write the connection down, since it is the answer to the tick database question you will be asked.


 10 min Add the second effect: measure a random access pattern over the same array against a sequential one, and report the ratio. Prefetching only helps when the access is predictable.

title: Day 277 — Which volatility trades have an edge, and what February 2018 did
text:
Tasks 60 min


 35 min Compare the three: selling a delta-hedged straddle, selling a variance swap, and holding a short VIX futures position. Simulate a fast volatility spike and report each one’s loss. They differ substantially because a variance swap’s payoff is quadratic in the move while a delta-hedged option’s is not, and a VIX future is a bet on the term structure rather than on realized variance at all.


 25 min Work through the February 2018 mechanics: an inverse volatility product rebalances to a constant short exposure daily, so a large volatility rise forces buying at the close into the move, which raises volatility further. Write the mechanism out and note that it is the same forced-deleveraging structure as day 13’s margin spiral.

 15 min Write the correct answer in three sentences: the price of a replicable claim equals the cost of its replicating portfolio, that cost happens to equal a discounted expectation under a particular measure, and that measure is the one under which the discounted stock is a martingale. Nobody is assumed to be risk neutral anywhere in that chain.


 10 min Check the invariance numerically: simulate the same paths under two drifts with identical volatility, and confirm that the quadratic variation, and hence the implied volatility, is unchanged. Volatility is the same under both measures and that is why it is the parameter you can estimate from prices.

title: Self-check
text:
Use each phase block on that phase’s milestone day. The final list is day 365.
The rule is the same throughout: say the answer out loud before you look. Recognising a correct explanation is easy and feels identical to knowing it, which is exactly why reading the answer is not a test. If the answer takes more than two minutes, you have not compressed it enough to use it in an interview.
Questions marked ★ are ones that get asked in buy-side interviews close to this form.

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 1 — Markets

★ A stock closes at $100, goes ex-dividend $2 overnight, and opens at $98. Your data vendor’s “adjusted close” series shows no gap. What exactly did the vendor do to the historical prices, and name one analysis that the adjustment silently breaks.
You are long one E-mini S&P future. Describe every cash flow between today and expiry, including the ones that happen daily. Now do the same for being long $1 notional of SPY.
Why does an ETF’s market price stay close to its net asset value? Name the mechanism and who is paid to run it.
★ You want to short a stock. Walk through what actually has to happen, who lends the shares, what you pay, and what can force you to close the position at the worst moment.
Futures are in contango. Explain what happens to a long position’s return when the contract is rolled, and why “contango means you lose money” is not quite right.
Name three distinct businesses that call themselves “quant” and describe how each one earns its revenue. Which of them is competing with you?

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 2 — Returns and noise

★ A strategy returns +50% then −50%. What is the arithmetic mean daily return, the geometric mean, and how much money do you have? Then state the general relationship between the two means and volatility.
Why do we use log returns for time aggregation and simple returns for cross-sectional aggregation? Give the one line of algebra behind each.
★ You have three years of daily returns and a realized Sharpe ratio of 1.0. Give a standard error for it. Can you reject a true Sharpe of 0?
Returns are close to uncorrelated but absolute returns are strongly autocorrelated. What does each of those two facts rule out, and what do they jointly imply about a model of returns?
★ You tested 200 strategy variants and the best has a Sharpe of 2.3. What do you now believe about its true Sharpe, and what is the calculation you would show to justify that belief?
State what the deflated Sharpe ratio deflates by, and what it assumes about the strategies you tried that is usually false.
Why is a block bootstrap the right resampling scheme for a return series, and what determines the block length?

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 3 — Time series

Define stationarity in the weak sense. Give one financial series that is plausibly stationary and one that is clearly not, and say what you do about the second.
★ Two independent random walks are regressed on each other. Describe what happens to the t-statistic and the R², and explain why. What is the fix?
ADF and KPSS have opposite null hypotheses. State both, and say what you conclude when they disagree.
★ Explain cointegration to someone who knows regression but not time series, in three sentences, and say why it is the thing pairs trading actually relies on.
Given an estimated Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process for a spread, derive the half-life and say how it should set your holding period. What goes wrong when the half-life is longer than your backtest?
What does a GARCH(1,1) actually assert about volatility, and what does the sum of its two coefficients tell you?
★ What is the Kalman filter doing, in one sentence with no matrices, and why would you use it for a hedge ratio instead of a rolling regression?

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 4 — Portfolios and risk

★ Mean-variance optimization is optimal and nobody runs it raw. Explain the contradiction, and say which input the result is most sensitive to.
You estimate a 500×500 covariance matrix from 750 daily observations. What is wrong with it, and what does Marchenko-Pastur tell you about which eigenvalues to trust?
Explain Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage to a geneticist in one sentence, using something they already do.
★ What is the difference between a risk factor and an alpha factor? Give an example of a factor that changed category over time.
A portfolio has 12% volatility and beta 0.9 to the market. Decompose its risk. What fraction is idiosyncratic, and what did you have to assume?
State the Kelly fraction for a simple bet, then say why practitioners run a fraction of it, in terms of what full Kelly does to the distribution of outcomes rather than to its mean.
★ VaR at 99% is $1M. Say precisely what that does and does not claim, and name the loss it is silent about.

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 5 — The research harness

★ Name five distinct ways look-ahead bias gets into a backtest, and for each, the test that catches it.
What does “point in time” mean for a fundamental data item, and what does a restatement do to a backtest that ignores it?
Your universe is today’s S&P 500 constituents, taken back ten years. Quantify, roughly, what that does to your results and say which direction it biases them.
Vectorized and event-driven backtests give different answers on the same strategy. Give two reasons that is expected and one that means you have a bug.
★ A strategy has a Sharpe of 2.0 before costs and 0.3 after. What does that tell you about its turnover and its likely capacity, and what is the first thing you would change?
Describe a unit test that makes look-ahead impossible rather than merely undetected.

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 6 — Alpha

★ Define the information coefficient. Relate it to the information ratio, and state the assumptions in the relationship you just used.
Your signal has an IC of 0.03. Is that good? Answer in terms of breadth and turnover rather than in the abstract.
Why neutralize a signal against sector and market beta before evaluating it, and what are you throwing away when you do?
★ Momentum and value are negatively correlated. Explain why that makes the combination better than either, quantitatively, and say what would break the argument.
Take one classic anomaly that has decayed since publication. Give the evidence for decay and the two competing explanations for it.
What is the capacity of a signal, how would you estimate it, and why is it not a property of the signal alone?
★ You have two signals with the same IC and correlation 0.8 between them. How do you weight them, and what happens to that answer as the correlation approaches 1?

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 7 — Machine learning

★ Standard k-fold cross-validation is wrong on financial data. Give two separate reasons, and describe purging and embargoing as the fixes for each.
What does the triple-barrier method label, and what problem with fixed-horizon labels does it solve?
Overlapping labels break an assumption that most estimators rely on. Which one, and what is the standard correction?
★ Your gradient boosting model beats ridge regression by 15% in cross-validated R² and loses to it out of sample. Give three explanations and say how you would distinguish them.
Why is feature importance from a tree ensemble misleading here, and what do you compute instead?
You are using a language model on earnings-call transcripts. Name the leak that is specific to pretrained models and does not exist when you build your own features.
★ What signal-to-noise ratio should you expect on daily equity returns, and how does that change the model class you should reach for?

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 8 — Derivatives

★ State Itô’s lemma and say, in words, what the extra term is doing that ordinary calculus does not have.
Derive Black-Scholes by replication. You should be able to do this on a whiteboard in ten minutes. Then say where the real-world drift went.
What does “risk-neutral” mean? Common wrong answer: that investors are risk neutral. Say what is actually being claimed.
★ You are short a straddle and delta hedging continuously. Where does your profit and loss come from? Write it as a relationship between implied and realized volatility.
Gamma and theta have opposite signs for a reason. State it, and say what that implies about a position that is long gamma in a quiet market.
Why does the implied volatility surface slope downward in strike for equity indices, and give two explanations that are not the same explanation restated.
★ Local volatility and stochastic volatility both fit today’s surface. Name something they disagree about, and say which observable would tell them apart.
The variance risk premium is persistently positive. What is the trade, why is it not free money, and what happened to people running it in February 2018?

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 9 — Microstructure

★ Explain adverse selection to a market maker’s grandmother, then say how the market maker prices it in.
What does Kyle’s lambda measure, and what does its magnitude tell you about how much you can trade?
Why is market impact closer to the square root of size than to linear? Give the empirical evidence and one mechanism.
★ Your backtest assumed fills at the mid. Estimate what that assumption cost you for a strategy trading 1% of daily volume, and say which components you are counting.
Describe implementation shortfall, and say what it captures that VWAP slippage does not.
Name three things a high-frequency firm does that you cannot do, and one advantage you have that they do not.

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 10 — Production

★ Roughly how long does an L1 cache reference take, a main memory reference, a random SSD read, and a round trip across a data centre? Now say why the answer changes how you would store a tick database.
Your daily pipeline silently produced yesterday’s signal today. Which monitor would have caught it, and why is “the job succeeded” not that monitor?
What does reconciliation compare, how often, and what do you do when it disagrees?
Explain to a C++ programmer why your Python is slow, and name the two changes that would help most.
★ Write, or describe precisely, a SQL query that computes a 20-day rolling mean per symbol from a trades table. Then say why doing it in SQL rather than pandas might be the right call.
Your strategy has been live for six weeks and is underperforming the backtest by 40 basis points a month. List the diagnoses in the order you would test them.

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 11 — The interview

★ Two players alternate flipping a fair coin; the first to get heads wins. What is the probability the first player wins? Now they need two heads in a row.
★ A stick breaks at two uniform random points. Probability the pieces form a triangle. Do it by sample space, not simulation.
★ You are shown a random variable’s realizations one at a time and must stop on the largest. What is the optimal policy and its success probability?
★ Explain the bias-variance trade-off in ninety seconds, out loud, without the word “trade-off”.
★ I am making a market in the number of gas stations in the United States. Give me a two-sided quote and defend the width.
★ Why are you leaving academia? Three sentences. A researcher at the firm has to find it convincing, not polite.
★ Present your genetics research in five minutes to someone who is smart, quantitative, and knows no biology. Which single result do you lead with?

title: Self-check
text:
Phase 12 — The whole year
The list the year was designed around. Answer without notes.

What is the difference between a price and a return, and why does almost every mistake in this field start there?
Where does a systematic strategy’s edge come from? Name the three broad sources and give an example of each.
★ How much evidence does it take to believe a backtest? Give the number from milestone 2 and the reasoning behind it.
Why is transaction cost the thing that decides whether a strategy exists?
What does a factor model buy you that a covariance matrix does not?
★ When is machine learning the right tool here, and when is it a more expensive way to overfit?
Why does an option’s value depend on volatility and not on expected return?
Who is on the other side of your trade, and what do they know that you don’t?
What is your strategy’s capacity, and what happens at twice that size?
★ What would make you stop running this strategy tomorrow?

And four you should be able to do, not just say:

Build a point-in-time backtest of a signal from raw data, with costs, in an afternoon.
Derive Black-Scholes by replication on a whiteboard.
Take an interview probability question you have not seen, and get to the right answer out loud while someone watches.
State, about your own year of work, which result you are least confident in and why.

Anything on this page you cannot answer is not a failure. It is the reading list for the autumn.

text:
Tasks 60 min


 30 min Derive the link rather than quoting it: regressing the spread change on its lagged level gives a coefficient that maps to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck reversion speed, and the half-life is the log of two over that speed.  15 min Set the thresholds from the model: the fitted stationary standard deviation gives the natural scale, so entry at two of those and exit at zero is derived rather than chosen. Implement it in qlib/signals/pairs.py.


 15 min Map the surface anyway and report it: entry from 1.0 to 3.0, exit from minus 0.5 to 1.0, Sharpe plotted as a surface with your derived point marked. A flat surface means the rule is robust; a sharp peak elsewhere is the thing to distrust. Every point logs to research_log.jsonl.

 20 min Write the argument out: a model trained on text through some date has seen commentary about the outcomes of events in your backtest window, so a sentiment score it produces for a 2019 filing is not a 2019 sentiment score.  30 min Design the detection experiment: score filings with the model and check whether its apparent skill is higher on well-known events than on obscure ones, or higher on large caps than small, holding the actual predictability constant as far as you can.  15 min Write the policy for the book: where a language model is the right tool, which is summarising or extracting a structured field from unstructured text, and where it is not, which is producing a judgement about an outcome. Extraction is much harder to contaminate than prediction.

title: Day 294 — The microstructure models, closed book
text:
Drill interview thread
Spaced repetition, not cramming. Every drill in the year is collected on the drills page.


 Timed mixed set, third sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score and compare against the last two.


 A trading game: I flip a coin twenty times and you may buy or sell a contract that pays the number of heads. I quote you 9 at 11. What do you do, and how does your answer change if I quote 9 at 11 after seeing the first five flips and you have not?


 The million dollar question, first attempt: what would you do with a million dollars? Answer out loud in ninety seconds. The bad answers are a fund’s marketing pitch or a personal finance plan; the good answer says something about how you think about risk and time.

text:
Tasks 60 min


 35 min Write the two-page version of the platform, the alpha book and the option pricer: what it is, one figure, the result with its interval, the specification count where relevant, and the limitation you consider most serious. Method goes in a short section rather than at the front.

text:
The running strategy

The three write-ups are the form in which the year’s work actually gets read: result first, one figure, interval, specification count, and the most serious limitation, each in two pages.

What you should be able to do tonight

Write and send three outreach messages, each referencing something specific the recipient did.
State what you are asking for, which is a conversation rather than a job.

title: Day 354 — Outreach that is worth the recipient’s two minutes
text:
Tasks 60 min


 30 min Write three messages, each under 150 words: who you are in one sentence, the specific thing of theirs you read and one real question about it, what you have built this year in one clause, and a clear small ask. The question about their work is what makes it a message rather than a request.


 20 min Send them, and set up the follow-up discipline: a tracker with the date sent, the ask, and a follow-up date two weeks out. Then write the two-sentence follow-up now, while you are not disappointed, because writing it later is harder.


 10 min Draft the version for people you do not know at all, which is a different message: shorter, with a link to one write-up rather than an attachment, and a smaller ask.

title: Day 356 — How an offer is actually structured and what moves
section: What you should be able to do tonight

What you should be able to do tonight

State the components of a quantitative research offer and which are negotiable.
State what creates leverage and what you would do with an exploding offer.

title: Day 356 — How an offer is actually structured and what moves
text:
Tasks 65 min


 30 min Write out the structure: base, sign-on, guaranteed first-year bonus, discretionary bonus, deferred compensation and its vesting, and any non-compete. The sign-on and the guarantee move most easily, the base moves within a band, and the deferral schedule is usually firm. The non-compete is the term that most affects your next five years and the one candidates ignore.


 25 min Plan the timing: leverage comes from parallel processes finishing near each other, which means starting applications in a batch rather than sequentially. Write your target application window and the sequencing, and note what you would say to an exploding offer, which is a specific sentence rather than a strategy.


 10 min Write the two-sentence version of what you would accept and what you would decline, so the decision is made before the pressure rather than during it.

title: Day 358 — The track record, reported without adjustment
text:
Tasks 65 min


 30 min Produce the track record table: monthly returns with no month omitted, cumulative return, realised volatility, maximum drawdown, and turnover. Then attach the Sharpe standard error at this sample length from qlib/stats.py, which will be wide enough that the point estimate carries almost no information, and say so on the same page rather than in a footnote.


 25 min Reconcile it against the broker: the account’s own statements against your engine’s derived positions and cash, using the day 327 reconciliation. Any difference that cannot be explained goes into the report as an unexplained residual rather than being absorbed into a rounding line.


 10 min Write the one-sentence statement of what this record supports, which is that the system runs and produces the positions it intends, rather than that the strategy works.
