title: Every drill
text:
Interview preparation is not a phase you do at the end. Probability under pressure decays if you touch it once; it sticks if you touch it fifty times. Every seventh day carries a drill, and they accumulate here.
52 drill sittings across the year.

title: Every drill
text:
Markets
Day 7 · Thu 13 Aug

Mental arithmetic baseline, and you will repeat this every drill day for a year, so write the numbers down. Ten two-digit multiplications against a 60-second clock, then 1/7 through 6/7 as decimals from memory, then 15 percent of 340 and 340 divided by 8. Record the time and the error count.
Counting, warm-up: how many distinct five-card poker hands contain exactly one pair? Get the number, then check it sums correctly against the total of 2,598,960 hands when you add the other categories from memory.
Conditional probability, the version that gets asked: a family has two children, at least one of whom is a boy born on a Tuesday. Probability both are boys? Do it by enumerating the sample space, and then say out loud why the Tuesday changes the answer at all.

Day 14 · Thu 20 Aug

Arithmetic, timed as before: ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, then 12 percent of 425 and 7 divided by 16 as a decimal. Compare the time to day 7 and write both numbers down.
Bayes, in the form interviewers use: a test for a condition present in 1 in 1,000 people has 99 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity. Positive test, what is the posterior? Do it in your head with natural frequencies out of 100,000, not with the formula.
Now the version they follow up with: how good would specificity have to be for the posterior to exceed one half? Solve it algebraically, out loud.

Day 21 · Thu 27 Aug

Arithmetic, timed: ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, plus 1/12 and 1/16 as decimals. Three data points now. Plot them at the end of the month, not today.
Expectation by indicators, which is the trick behind half of the canon: shuffle a deck of 52 cards. What is the expected number of cards in their original position? Get it in one line using linearity, then say why the answer does not depend on the deck size.
The follow-up they ask: what is the probability that no card is in its original position, and what number does it approach? You should recognise this one; state the limit and where it comes from.

Day 28 · Thu 3 Sep

Arithmetic, timed, fourth sitting: ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, then 1/13 to three places and 17 times 23 in your head. Now plot the four times you have recorded. The trend is the point.
Symmetry, the argument that replaces a calculation: two players alternate flipping a fair coin, first to get heads wins. Probability the first player wins? Solve it with a one-line symmetry or recursion argument rather than summing the series.
The follow-up: same game, but you need two heads in a row to win. Set up the recursion and solve it. Say out loud which states you need and why there are exactly three.

title: Every drill
text:
Returns and noise
Day 35 · Thu 10 Sep

Arithmetic, timed: ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, then 3/8, 5/16 and 1/11 as decimals. Fifth sitting. Compare against the plot you made last night.
The urn canon: an urn has 5 red and 7 blue balls; you draw 3 without replacement. Probability all three are the same colour? Do it two ways, by counting and by the multiplication rule, and check they agree.
Variance by conditioning: you roll a die, then flip that many coins. What is the expected number of heads and its variance? Use the law of total variance and say out loud which term is which.

Day 42 · Thu 17 Sep

Arithmetic, timed, sixth sitting: ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, then 2/7 times 3/8 as a decimal without writing anything down.
The classic they open with: 100 people board a plane, the first sits at random, everyone after sits in their own seat if free and at random otherwise. Probability the last passenger gets their own seat? Answer by symmetry in under a minute, then justify the symmetry out loud.
Conditional expectation, geometric flavour: you flip a fair coin until you see HH. Expected number of flips? Set up the states, solve, then do the same for HT and say out loud why the two answers differ.

Day 49 · Thu 24 Sep

Arithmetic, timed, seventh sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, then 1.05 to the 12th power to two decimal places, approximated in your head.
Order statistics, a first look: draw three independent uniforms on the unit interval. What is the expected value of the largest? Of the middle one? Get the general formula for the kth of n and say out loud why the answers are equally spaced.
The trading-flavoured version they actually ask: two people each draw a uniform on the unit interval, see only their own, and may swap once if both agree. Should you ever agree to swap? Explain the adverse selection in two sentences.

Day 56 · Thu 1 Oct

Arithmetic, timed, eighth sitting: ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 1/1.05 to four decimal places by long division in your head.
The canonical urn-and-information problem: three cards, one red on both sides, one white on both sides, one red and white. You draw one at random and see red. Probability the other side is red? Say the wrong answer out loud first, then the right one, and name the mistake in the wrong one.
Expectation with a twist: you roll a fair die repeatedly and stop when you choose. Your payoff is the last roll. What is the optimal stopping rule and its expected value? Then do it for a payoff of the average of all rolls so far.

Day 63 · Thu 8 Oct

Arithmetic, timed, ninth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and the square root of 2, 3 and 5 to three decimal places from memory.
Symmetry and conditioning combined: a fair coin is flipped 100 times. Given that the first 50 flips contained 30 heads, what is the expected total number of heads? Then, given that the total was 60 heads, what is the expected number in the first 50? Say why the two questions are not the same shape.
Two months of drills have accumulated. Write down the three problem types that have been slowest for you so far. That list is the thing you actually track, not any individual answer.

title: Every drill
text:
Time series
Day 70 · Thu 15 Oct

Arithmetic, timed, tenth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 7 percent compounded for 10 years as a multiple, in your head.
The counting problem that separates people: how many ways can you arrange the letters of MISSISSIPPI? Then, what fraction of those arrangements have no two S adjacent? Do the second by placing the non-S letters first.
Conditional probability with a trap: you are told one of two coins is fair and the other is two-headed. You pick one, flip it three times, and get three heads. Probability you picked the two-headed coin? Then say what the answer approaches after ten heads and why it never reaches 1.

Day 77 · Thu 22 Oct

Arithmetic, timed, eleventh sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 1/64, 1/128 and 1/256 as decimals.
Bayes with a base rate that moves: a coin is fair with probability 0.9 and biased to 0.75 heads otherwise. You see 8 heads in 10 flips. Posterior that it is biased? Set it up with likelihood ratios rather than with the full formula.
Expectation, geometric: on average, how many times do you have to roll a fair die to see all six faces? Get the answer by decomposing into six waiting times, then say the general formula for n faces and its growth rate.

Day 84 · Thu 29 Oct

Arithmetic, timed, twelfth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 13 squared through 19 squared from memory.
The interview classic on symmetry and stopping: you flip a fair coin repeatedly. What is the expected number of flips to see HTH? Compare against HHH and say which is longer and why, out loud, without writing the Markov chain.
A counting problem with structure: how many distinct paths are there from one corner of an 8 by 8 grid to the opposite corner moving only right and up? Then how many stay weakly below the diagonal? Name the second number.

Day 91 · Thu 5 Nov

Arithmetic, timed, thirteenth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 2 to the 10th through 2 to the 16th from memory.
Variance decomposition under conditioning: a stock’s daily return has volatility that is 1 percent on 80 percent of days and 3 percent on the rest. What is the unconditional volatility, and the unconditional kurtosis? The second answer is the mechanism behind week 6.
Three months of drills. Write down the three problem types that are still slowest, compare against the list you made on day 63, and note what has moved.

Day 98 · Thu 12 Nov

Arithmetic, timed, fourteenth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 15 percent of 84 and 84 divided by 7 in your head.
Random walks start here, and they run for the next thirteen weeks. Gambler’s ruin: you start with 10 units, bet one unit per fair coin flip, and stop at 0 or 20. Probability you reach 20? Now do it when the coin pays out with probability 0.49 and say how much the answer moves.
Expected duration of the same game, which is the part people forget: how many flips on average before the fair version ends? Derive it from the difference equation rather than quoting the product.

title: Every drill
text:
Portfolios and risk
Day 105 · Thu 19 Nov

Arithmetic, timed, fifteenth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 1.02 to the 36th power approximated in your head.
Random walk, first passage: a symmetric random walk starts at 0. What is the probability it ever reaches plus 5? Now what is the expected time to do so? Say the second answer out loud before you compute it, and notice that it is surprising.
Optional stopping, gently: you flip a fair coin and win one unit for heads, lose one for tails. You stop when you are up 1 unit. Is this a winning strategy? Say precisely which assumption of optional stopping fails, and what a broker would call the thing that makes it fail.

Day 112 · Thu 26 Nov

Arithmetic, timed, sixteenth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 1/0.85 and 1/1.15 to three decimals.
Martingales and optional stopping: a gambler with 100 units bets one unit on fair coin flips and stops at 0 or 200. Use the martingale property to get the ruin probability in one line, then say which of the optional stopping conditions you relied on.
The version with a drift: same game, but the coin pays with probability 0.48. Find the martingale that works here and use it. This one is asked directly and the trick is finding the right exponential.

Day 119 · Thu 3 Dec

Arithmetic, timed, seventeenth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 45 times 45, 35 times 35 and 65 times 65 using the trick for numbers ending in 5.
Order statistics under a clock: n independent uniforms on the unit interval. What is the expected value of the maximum, the minimum, and the range? Then the expected gap between the largest and second largest, and what happens to it as n grows.
The trading version: 20 traders each independently quote a price drawn from the same distribution, and you trade against the best quote. What is the expected quality of the price you get, and why does that make you cautious rather than pleased?

Day 126 · Thu 10 Dec

Arithmetic, timed, eighteenth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 1/3, 2/9 and 5/6 as decimals plus their reciprocals.
Poisson processes: buses arrive as a Poisson process with mean gap 10 minutes. You arrive at a random time. What is your expected wait, and what is the expected length of the gap you land in? Explain the inspection paradox out loud.
The follow-up they use to check you understood: what is the expected time since the last bus? Give it without computing anything new.

Day 133 · Thu 17 Dec

Arithmetic, timed, nineteenth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 1.1 to the 7th and 0.9 to the 7th to three decimals.
Markov chains under a clock: a frog on a 5-lily-pad cycle jumps left or right with equal probability. Expected time to visit every pad? Then the stationary distribution if the jumps are 2 to 1 in one direction.
Expected value game, the kind that opens a trading interview: I roll a fair die and you may pay to see the result and then choose to reroll once, keeping the second. What is the game worth? Now with two rerolls, and say how you would compute it for n.

title: Every drill
text:
The research harness
Day 140 · Thu 24 Dec

Arithmetic, timed, twentieth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 1/7 through 1/13 to three decimals.
Random walk maximum: a symmetric random walk runs for 100 steps. What is the expected maximum? Use the reflection principle to get the distribution of the maximum first, and say the argument out loud rather than writing it.
Arcsine law, stated as an interview question: over a long fair coin-flipping game, what is the most likely fraction of time spent ahead? Most people say one half. Say the right answer and the shape of the distribution.

Day 147 · Thu 31 Dec

Arithmetic, timed, twenty-first sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 17 times 18, 23 times 27 and 34 times 36 using the complements trick.
Markov chains: a mouse in a 3 by 3 grid of rooms moves to a uniformly chosen adjacent room each minute, starting in a corner. Expected time to reach the centre? Set up the states using symmetry so there are three, not nine.
The follow-up: what is the long-run fraction of time spent in the centre? Get it from the stationary distribution and say why it is proportional to the number of doors.

Day 154 · Thu 7 Jan

Arithmetic, timed, twenty-second sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 250 divided by 7, 400 divided by 13 and 1000 divided by 17 to one decimal.
Optional stopping applied to a game: you draw cards one at a time from a shuffled deck and may stop at any point, winning if the next card is red. What is the best strategy and its value? The answer is surprising and the argument is a martingale one.
Expected value under a budget: you may pay to roll a die up to three times, keeping the last roll. What is the game worth, and what are the two thresholds in the optimal policy? State both numbers.

Day 161 · Thu 14 Jan

Arithmetic, timed, twenty-third sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 8 percent of 1,250 plus 12 percent of 3,400 in your head.
Random walks and stopping, combined: a symmetric random walk starts at 0 and you stop when you first hit plus 3 or minus 5. Probability of each, expected duration, and then the same for a walk with steps of plus 2 and minus 1 with equal probability.
Halfway through the drill thread’s second band. Write down the three problem types that are still slowest and compare against your day 91 list.

title: Every drill
text:
Alpha
Day 168 · Thu 21 Jan

Arithmetic, timed, twenty-fourth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 1.5 to the 10th power approximated to two significant figures.
Markov chain with an absorbing state: a tennis game is at deuce and each point is won independently with probability p. What is the probability of winning the game from deuce? Derive it, then evaluate at p of 0.55 and note how much the advantage amplifies.
The same amplification, asked as a trading question: your edge per trade is 51 to 49. Over a match structure that requires winning by two, what does your edge become? Say what the analogy is to compounding a small per-trade edge.

Day 175 · Thu 28 Jan

Arithmetic, timed, twenty-fifth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and the square roots of 250, 500 and 1,000 to two decimals.
Order statistics with a decision attached: you interview candidates one at a time in random order and must hire on the spot. What policy maximises the chance of hiring the best, and what is that chance? State the threshold rule and the limiting probability.
The trading version, which is how it is actually asked: you can trade once against a stream of quotes arriving in random order. When do you take one? Say why the answer is the same problem and what changes if you may take the second best.

Day 182 · Thu 4 Feb

Arithmetic, timed, twenty-sixth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 3 percent compounded over 25 years as a multiple.
Poisson and Markov combined, the last of this band: orders arrive at a market maker as a Poisson process at 10 per minute, each equally likely to be a buy or a sell. What is the distribution of net inventory after a minute, and its standard deviation? Then the probability inventory exceeds 5 in either direction.
Six months of drills. Write down the three problem types still slowest and compare against day 161. From next week the drill moves to statistics, machine learning and coding questions, so this is the last purely probabilistic sitting for a while.

Day 189 · Thu 11 Feb

Arithmetic, timed, twenty-seventh sitting, and it continues all year. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
The drill band changes today. Explain the bias-variance decomposition out loud in ninety seconds, then answer the follow-up they always ask: where does the irreducible error go, and why does more data not remove it? Record yourself once and listen to it.
Then the version aimed at this field: your model has an out-of-sample R-squared of 0.005 on daily returns. Is it useless? Answer in terms of information ratio rather than in terms of R-squared, and do the arithmetic out loud.

Day 196 · Thu 18 Feb

Arithmetic, timed, twenty-eighth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
Ridge against lasso, out loud in ninety seconds, including what each does to correlated predictors and which one you would pick for a factor model with 60 correlated signals. Then the follow-up: what does elastic net add, and why is it usually the right default here?
A coding question of the kind asked in a first round: given a list of trades with timestamps, symbols and quantities, compute the running position per symbol and the maximum absolute position reached. Write it in Python without pandas, in under ten minutes, and then say its complexity.

Day 203 · Thu 25 Feb

Arithmetic, timed, twenty-ninth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
Cross-validation out loud in ninety seconds: what it estimates, why the estimate is biased, and the two distinct reasons standard k-fold is wrong on financial data. You will build the fixes next week, so today is the explanation rather than the method.
Start the research presentation thread, which runs until July. Write the single sentence that states the most interesting result of your genetics work to someone quantitative who knows no biology. One sentence, out loud, timed. You will rewrite it perhaps twenty times over the next five months.

title: Every drill
text:
Machine learning
Day 210 · Thu 4 Mar

Arithmetic, timed, thirtieth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
The cross-validation question as asked, out loud in ninety seconds: why is k-fold wrong on financial data, and what are purging and embargoing? Then the follow-up: does that fix apply to a cross-sectional daily model with a one-day label, and why does the answer surprise people?
A SQL problem of first-round difficulty: from a trades table with timestamp, symbol, price and quantity, write a query giving the volume-weighted average price per symbol per day, and then the top three symbols by dollar volume on each day. The second half needs a window function; write it without looking it up.

Day 217 · Thu 11 Mar

Arithmetic, timed, thirty-first sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
Regularisation out loud in ninety seconds: what ridge does to correlated predictors, what lasso does differently, and what the penalty is actually buying you in terms of bias and variance. Then the question they follow with: how would you choose the penalty when your folds are not independent?
A Python problem at second-round difficulty: implement a function that, given a list of (timestamp, price) ticks and a window in seconds, returns the rolling maximum efficiently. The naive version is quadratic; write the linear one with a deque and say why it is linear.

Day 224 · Thu 18 Mar

Arithmetic, timed, thirty-second sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
The model comparison question, out loud: your boosting model wins in cross-validation and loses out of sample. Give three explanations and say how you would distinguish them. Then say which one you would bet on for daily equity returns and why.
Research presentation, second sitting: take the one-sentence result from day 203 and expand it to sixty seconds. No biology vocabulary that a physicist would not know. Time it and note where you exceeded the budget.

Day 231 · Thu 25 Mar

Arithmetic, timed, thirty-third sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
A statistics question they use to separate people: you fit a model, it looks good, and you want to know whether to believe it. Walk through what you would check, in order, in two minutes. There are at least six checks and the order matters.
A Python problem: given two sorted lists of trade timestamps from two venues, find all pairs within 50 milliseconds of each other, in linear time. Write it, then say what changes if the lists are not sorted.

Day 238 · Thu 1 Apr

Arithmetic, timed, thirty-fourth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
The whole machine learning round, compressed: bias and variance, regularisation, cross-validation on dependent data, and why more capacity does not help at low signal-to-noise. Four answers, ninety seconds each, out loud, against a clock.
Research presentation, third sitting: expand to two minutes, and this time include one number with its uncertainty. Time it. The number with the uncertainty is what makes a quantitative audience trust the rest.

title: Every drill
text:
Derivatives
Day 245 · Thu 8 Apr

Arithmetic, timed, thirty-fifth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
A statistics question asked in exactly this form: you have two estimators of the same quantity, one unbiased with high variance and one biased with low variance. How do you choose? Answer with mean squared error and then say what changes if the estimate feeds a position size rather than a report.
A coding question: implement a function that computes the running median of a stream in better than linear time per update. Two heaps is the answer; write it, then say the complexity of insert and of query.

Day 252 · Thu 15 Apr

Arithmetic, timed, thirty-sixth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
A modelling question they ask to see how you think: you are given a dataset and asked to predict something with a 55 percent base rate. Walk through what you do in the first thirty minutes, out loud, in two minutes. There is a right ordering and it starts with looking at the data rather than at models.
Research presentation, fourth sitting: three minutes now, and add the methods sentence. One sentence on the method, not three. Time it.

Day 259 · Thu 22 Apr

Arithmetic, timed, thirty-seventh sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
A statistics question with a trap: you run an A/B test, it is not significant, and someone asks whether that means there is no effect. Answer properly in ninety seconds, including what you would report instead of a p-value. This gets asked because most candidates say the wrong thing in the first sentence.
A coding problem: given a stream of prices, implement an online estimator of the exponentially weighted mean and variance in one pass with no stored history. Write it, then say what happens numerically if the decay is very close to one.

Day 266 · Thu 29 Apr

Arithmetic, timed, thirty-eighth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
A statistics question in the form they use: you have 500 features and 1,000 observations and you want to know which features matter. Walk through your approach in two minutes, out loud. Then answer the follow-up: how would your answer change if the observations were a time series?
Research presentation, fifth sitting: four minutes now, with one figure described verbally. Describe the figure in words as if the listener cannot see it, which is a skill worth having for a phone screen.

Day 273 · Thu 6 May

Arithmetic, timed, thirty-ninth sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications and the sevenths.
The last statistics sitting of this band. You have thirty seconds to say why a model that fits well in sample may be worse than one that fits badly, and ninety seconds to give a concrete example from your own year’s work. Use the machine learning audit from day 233.
A coding question at the harder end: given a large file of trades that does not fit in memory, compute the median trade size. Say the approach out loud before writing anything; there are at least two reasonable answers and the difference is exactness against memory.

Day 280 · Thu 13 May

The drill band changes today and runs under a clock from here to July. Timed mixed set: five problems in fifteen minutes, drawn from probability, expectation and mental arithmetic, with no warning about which is which. Score yourself out of five and write it down; this number is what you are tracking now.
Market making, first sitting: I am making a market in the number of piano tuners in Chicago. Give me a two-sided quote and defend the width. Then I trade with you and you must requote. The requoting is the part candidates get wrong.
Estimation: how many options contracts trade on SPY in a day? Get within a factor of three by reasoning, not recall, then check against the Cboe market statistics page.

title: Every drill
text:
Microstructure
Day 287 · Thu 20 May

Timed mixed set, second sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes across probability, expectation and arithmetic. Score out of five and compare against day 280.
Market making, second sitting: I make a market in the sum of two dice, and you must quote me a two-sided market in the sum before either is rolled. Then I trade with you and one die is revealed. Requote. Say your reasoning out loud at every step, because the reasoning is what is being assessed.
The question every academic answers badly, first attempt: why are you leaving academia? Three sentences, out loud, recorded. Listen to it once. You will rewrite this perhaps thirty times before July and the first version is always defensive.

Day 294 · Thu 27 May

Timed mixed set, third sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score and compare against the last two.
A trading game: I flip a coin twenty times and you may buy or sell a contract that pays the number of heads. I quote you 9 at 11. What do you do, and how does your answer change if I quote 9 at 11 after seeing the first five flips and you have not?
The million dollar question, first attempt: what would you do with a million dollars? Answer out loud in ninety seconds. The bad answers are a fund’s marketing pitch or a personal finance plan; the good answer says something about how you think about risk and time.

Day 301 · Thu 3 Jun

Timed mixed set, fourth sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score and plot the four scores you have.
Market making with inventory: I make a market in a stock and you trade with me three times in the same direction. Each time, requote and say what you are doing to your mid and to your width, and why. This is your day 25 inventory simulation asked verbally.
Estimation: what is the daily dollar volume of the US equity market? Reason to it from index market capitalisation and turnover rather than recalling it, then check against any public figure you can find.

Day 308 · Thu 10 Jun

Timed mixed set, fifth sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score, and plot all five scores. The trend is what matters.
Market making under adverse selection: I make a market in a stock and you may trade with me, but you know one piece of information I do not. How should I set my width, and how should you trade to avoid revealing what you know? Argue both sides out loud.
Why are you leaving academia, second attempt. Compare against your day 287 recording. The improvement to aim for is fewer words about what is wrong with academia and more about what the work you want is.

title: Every drill
text:
Production
Day 315 · Thu 17 Jun

Timed mixed set, sixth sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score and plot.
A SQL problem at the harder end: from a positions table with daily snapshots per symbol, write a query that finds, for each symbol, the longest consecutive run of days it was held. Gaps and islands is the pattern; write it with window functions.
Research presentation, sixth sitting: five minutes, the full version, timed. Record it. This is the first time you should be at full length and it will be too long.

Day 322 · Thu 24 Jun

Timed mixed set, seventh sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score and plot.
A systems question: you need to store five years of tick data for 500 symbols and query arbitrary time ranges. Describe your storage design in two minutes, out loud, with the latency numbers behind each choice. This is a question with no single right answer and the reasoning is what is scored.
Market making, fourth sitting: I quote a market in a quantity you can estimate better than I can. Trade with me, then tell me what you learned from the fact that I was willing to trade at that price.

Day 329 · Thu 1 Jul

Timed mixed set, eighth sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score and plot all eight.
A production question: your strategy has been live six weeks and is underperforming the backtest by 40 basis points a month. List the diagnoses in the order you would test them, out loud, in two minutes. There is a correct ordering and it starts with the cheapest checks.
Why are you leaving academia, third attempt, recorded. Compare against days 287 and 308. By now it should be under forty-five seconds and should contain one concrete thing about the work rather than about the institution.

title: Every drill
text:
The interview
Day 336 · Thu 8 Jul

Timed mixed set, ninth sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes, and this one is on top of today’s thirty-minute set, so you are working tired. That is deliberate; the fourth interview of a superday is also tired.
Market making, fifth sitting: I quote you a market on a quantity with a known distribution, and you may trade any size up to a limit. How much do you trade, and how does size depend on your edge? The size answer is Kelly and you have already done that arithmetic on day 128.
Estimation: how many people are airborne over the United States right now? Reason to it, then say which of your assumptions the answer is most sensitive to.

Day 343 · Thu 15 Jul

Timed mixed set, tenth sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score and plot all ten.
Market making, sixth sitting, with a twist: I trade with you and then tell you I will trade again in the same direction regardless of your quote. What do you do? The answer is not obvious and saying why out loud is the exercise.
The million dollar question, second attempt. Compare against day 294. A good answer says something about the horizon you would run it over and the drawdown you would accept, both of which you computed on day 129.

Day 350 · Thu 22 Jul

Timed mixed set, eleventh sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score and plot all eleven.
A full mock round, first attempt: fifteen minutes of mixed probability, market making and a behavioural question, in one sitting, with no breaks between them. The transitions are what is being practised.
Estimation under adversarial follow-up: give a Fermi estimate, then defend it when told it is wrong by a factor of ten. The correct response identifies which assumption would have to be wrong, rather than revising the answer.

Day 357 · Thu 29 Jul

Timed mixed set, twelfth sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score, plot all twelve, and compare against the target you set on day 330.
Full mock round, second attempt: fifteen minutes, mixed, cold. Compare against day 350 and note whether the transitions have improved.
The academia question, fourth and final rehearsed attempt, recorded. Play days 287, 308, 329 and today in sequence and keep whichever is best rather than the most recent.

title: Every drill
text:
Capstone
Day 364 · Thu 5 Aug

Timed mixed set, thirteenth and final scored sitting: five problems in fifteen minutes. Score, and compare against the target you set on day 330.
One last full mock: fifteen minutes, mixed, cold, recorded. Compare against day 350 and day 357.
Then stop and read the fifty-two drill entries on the drills page in order. It takes ten minutes and it is the clearest record you have of how much ground a year of twenty-minute sittings covers.

title: 365-Day Quant Bootcamp
text:
What this is
One year, one hour a day. Three hundred and sixty-five consecutive days, each sized for about sixty focused minutes, six of them working and every seventh lighter.
It is built for a specific starting point: you already have PhD-level statistics, instrumental variables, massive multiple testing, high-dimensional covariance, and fluent Python. You have no finance. So the year does not re-teach probability, and it does not go easy on the parts you have never seen — the plumbing of markets, stochastic calculus, cointegration, order books, and the specific ways a backtest lies to you.
The target role is buy-side quantitative researcher — statistical arbitrage and machine-learning alpha, the kind of seat at Two Sigma, D. E. Shaw, Citadel, a Millennium pod, AQR or Point72. It is the track where your existing training transfers hardest. A Mendelian randomization study is instrumental variable estimation. A genome-wide scan is the multiple-testing problem that kills most published trading strategies. A linkage-disequilibrium matrix is an ill-conditioned covariance matrix. You are not starting from zero; you are starting from the wrong vocabulary.

title: 365-Day Quant Bootcamp
text:
The bargain this makes
An hour a day is a real constraint, and it buys a real thing: after 365 hours you will have a system that trades, a portfolio of work you can show, and the ability to answer a quant interview question without bluffing. It does not buy you a shortcut. Nothing here promises returns, and several weeks are spent learning why most claimed returns are not real.

title: 365-Day Quant Bootcamp
text:
How a day works
Every day page has the same parts, in this order:



Part
What it’s for




Why today
One sentence on what this day unlocks. Read it before you start.


What you should be able to do tonight
Two or three checkable claims. Not “understand cointegration”.


Tasks
Two to four items with minute estimates that sum to about an hour. Tick them off; the page remembers.


Drill
Every seventh day only. Twenty minutes of interview preparation, all year, so it never becomes a cram.


The running strategy
On days that move the one system you are building. Collected on the strategy page.


Resources
Every link the day needs. Nothing to go hunting for.


Deliverable
The artifact you should have at the end — a file, a plot, a number, a paragraph.


Checkpoint
One question. If you can’t answer it without notes, you are not done.


Prepare for tomorrow
Ten minutes tonight. This is what the evening email sends you.

title: 365-Day Quant Bootcamp
text:
The twelve phases


Weeks 1–4 · Days 1–28 #### Markets Vocabulary and plumbing. What a share, a future, an option and a bond actually oblige you to do. Order types, matching, borrow, margin. Then market data, corporate actions, and a point-in-time store you built yourself.


Weeks 5–9 · Days 29–63 #### Returns and noise Log returns, fat tails, volatility clustering. Then the Sharpe ratio as an estimator, with a standard error — and the multiple-testing correction that decides whether a backtest means anything. This is your home turf under different names.


Weeks 10–14 · Days 64–98 #### Time series Stationarity, unit roots, spurious regression. Cointegration and the error-correction model, which is what pairs trading actually is. GARCH and realized volatility. Kalman filters for a hedge ratio that moves.


Weeks 15–19 · Days 99–133 #### Portfolios and risk Markowitz, and why nobody uses it raw. Shrinkage and random matrix theory on a covariance matrix that behaves exactly like an LD matrix. Factor models, risk decomposition, and Kelly sizing.


Weeks 20–23 · Days 134–161 #### The research harness The phase that separates people who backtest from people who research. Point-in-time data, the full taxonomy of look-ahead, event-driven architecture, transaction costs, and tests that make leakage impossible rather than unlikely.


Weeks 24–29 · Days 162–203 #### Alpha The core craft. Signal construction, information coefficient, decay, turnover, capacity. Value, momentum, quality and carry replicated honestly, including the ones that stopped working. Then combining them.


Weeks 30–34 · Days 204–238 #### Machine learning Why standard ML breaks on non-IID data with a signal-to-noise ratio two orders of magnitude below anything you have worked with. Purged and embargoed cross-validation. Triple-barrier labels. Then an honest verdict against the linear baseline.


Weeks 35–40 · Days 239–280 #### Derivatives The most formal mathematics of the year and the furthest from your training. Brownian motion, Itô’s lemma, Black-Scholes twice over, the greeks, delta hedging, the volatility surface, and the variance risk premium.


Weeks 41–44 · Days 281–308 #### Microstructure Who was on the other side of the closing price you assumed you traded at. Order books, adverse selection, Kyle’s lambda, the square-root impact law, and what your strategy’s capacity really is.


Weeks 45–47 · Days 309–329 #### Production SQL and Parquet properly. Enough C++ to read a matching engine and to know why it is fast. Then scheduling, logging, monitoring, reconciliation, and a paper account at a real broker.


Weeks 48–51 · Days 330–357 #### The interview By now the drill thread has run for eleven months, so this is consolidation, not a standing start. Probability under a clock, trading games, the research presentation, and the application campaign.


Week 52 · Days 358–365 #### Capstone The research dossier, the paper-traded track record you did not tamper with, and a written account of what you believed in September 2026 that turned out to be wrong.

title: 365-Day Quant Bootcamp
section: Six rules that make this work
text:
Six rules that make this work

An hour, every day, beats six hours on Saturday. The schedule is built around the fact that you have a job. The cost of a missed day is small; the cost of a missed fortnight is the whole thing.
Produce the deliverable. Every day names an artifact. A day that leaves nothing on disk did not happen, and eleven months from now the milestone reports are assembled from those artifacts.
Answer the checkpoint out loud. Ninety seconds. Recognising a correct explanation feels identical to knowing it, which is exactly why reading the answer is not a test.
Assume the result is not real until you have tried to kill it. You already do this. A backtested Sharpe of 2 is a p-value from an unreported number of hypotheses, and phases 2 and 5 exist to make that instinct quantitative.
The drill is not optional. Twenty minutes every seventh day for a year is fifty sittings. Four weeks of cramming in July 2027 is not a substitute and you will be able to tell.
Catch-up days are load-bearing. Every seventh day is deliberately not full. You will fall behind somewhere, and a year-long plan with no slack is a plan you abandon in November. If you are on track, take the day or go deeper — do not pull work forward into it by default.

title: 365-Day Quant Bootcamp
text:
The evening email
Every evening you get one email: what tomorrow is, and the two-to-four things worth doing tonight so tomorrow starts clean. Download the PDF, clone the repo, start the data pull, open the notebook. Nothing in it takes more than ten minutes. It is the same content as the Prepare for tomorrow block at the bottom of each day page.

title: 365-Day Quant Bootcamp
text:
Start here
Tonight: set up your environment — Python, the data stack, accounts, and the work repository. About an hour, and it is the difference between day 1 being a study day and day 1 being an afternoon of dependency errors.
Then: Day 1, or the full year. If you want to know what you are aiming at before you start, read the hiring page first — it is the least comfortable page on this site and the most useful one to read early.

title: The running strategy
text:
The days that teach and the days that build are the same days. From the first week you are assembling one system — data, signals, portfolio construction, costs, execution, monitoring — and by the capstone it is running on a schedule against a paper account with a track record you did not tamper with. This page is that thread pulled out of the calendar.
83 days move the system forward.

title: The running strategy
text:
Markets

Day 20 · Wed 26 Aug · The store, part one: schema and ingestion

The data store begins. qlib/store.py defines the schema and qlib/ingest.py fills it; every table carries both the date a fact refers to and the date you learned it, which is the constraint that makes point-in-time queries possible later rather than retrofitted.

Day 22 · Fri 28 Aug · The store, part two: adjustment as a view, not a column

The store can now return both a raw price series and a total-return series from the same rows, with adjustment computed at read time. That choice is what will let a backtest run in March against the same file you ingested in September without the history having quietly moved.

Day 23 · Sat 29 Aug · The store, part three: the test that makes as-of true

The as-of semantics are now enforced by two tests rather than by intention. This is the first instance of the pattern that week 23 generalises: leakage is prevented by construction and asserted by a test, never by remembering to be careful.

Day 28 · Thu 3 Sep · Milestone: the market map and a store that does not lie

Milestone 1 closes phase 1 with a working point-in-time daily store and a written account of what it cannot do. Every backtest for the rest of the year reads from qlib/store.py, and the limitations section is the list you check whenever a result looks better than it should.

title: The running strategy
text:
Returns and noise

Day 45 · Sun 20 Sep · Every performance number gets an interval from now on

The performance layer now reports intervals by default and has a coverage test behind them. From here, any strategy result in this course that appears without an interval is a bug rather than a style choice.

Day 53 · Mon 28 Sep · Implement the correction, and make the count automatic

The research log begins. Every strategy evaluation from today writes a line to research_log.jsonl, so the number of trials behind any later result is a fact you can count rather than a number you have to recall.

Day 60 · Mon 5 Oct · A simulator whose output passes your own stylized-facts test

qlib/simulate.py gives the project a null that is not a straw man. Any strategy result from here can be run against synthetic data with the same tails and clustering as the real thing, which is what makes a false-positive rate measurable rather than assumed.

Day 61 · Tue 6 Oct · The noise floor: one number you will be held to

qlib/noise.py fixes the evidence threshold for the whole year. Every later milestone reports its results against this number, which was computed before any of those results existed, and that ordering is what makes it a threshold rather than a rationalisation.

Day 63 · Thu 8 Oct · Milestone: the stylized facts and the noise floor

Milestone 2 sets the evidence bar for everything that follows. qlib/stats.py, qlib/simulate.py and qlib/noise.py are now the three modules that every later strategy result passes through before it is allowed to be called a result.

title: The running strategy
text:
Time series

Day 69 · Wed 14 Oct · The first strategy meets the noise floor

The first strategy in the book: a 12-month time-series momentum rule, evaluated against the noise floor from milestone 2 rather than against zero. The evaluation path it runs through is the one every later signal uses, so getting it right once is worth the hour.

Day 81 · Mon 26 Oct · The pair selection rule, written down before the results

qlib/signals/pairs.py holds the pair selection rule, fixed in code before any trading result exists, with its screen count logged automatically. The hurdle that count implies is on the first page of the milestone rather than in a footnote.

Day 82 · Tue 27 Oct · The half-life, and thresholds derived from it

The pairs rule takes its holding period and its thresholds from the fitted mean-reversion dynamics, and the parameter surface around that point is reported rather than hidden. Every point on the surface is a logged trial, which keeps the trial count honest.

Day 83 · Wed 28 Oct · The pairs backtest, with costs, in sample

The pairs strategy runs end to end with costs and produces a net Sharpe alongside a break-even cost curve. That curve becomes the standard chart for every strategy in the alpha book, because it says more than the headline number does.

Day 90 · Wed 4 Nov · Volatility targeting, and what it does and does not improve

The trend follower now sizes on a volatility forecast from qlib/vol.py rather than on constant notional, and the improvement is decomposed into the mechanical part and the forecast-quality part rather than claimed as a whole.

Day 93 · Sat 7 Nov · A hedge ratio that is allowed to move

The pairs strategy gains a dynamic hedge ratio estimated by maximum likelihood rather than a window length chosen by hand. The static version stays in the code as the comparison the milestone reports against.

Day 94 · Sun 8 Nov · Does the moving hedge ratio actually help, or just fit better

The dynamic and static hedge ratio versions of the pairs strategy are compared out of sample at matched turnover, so any improvement is attributable to the estimator rather than to trading more.

Day 96 · Tue 10 Nov · The out-of-sample run, once, on a period you never looked at

The pairs strategy is frozen in a committed configuration file and run once out of sample, with its result placed against the distribution the same procedure produces on synthetic data containing no relationships at all.

Day 98 · Thu 12 Nov · Milestone: a pairs strategy, and what it survived

Milestone 3 closes phase 3 with a complete strategy: selection rule, derived thresholds, dynamic hedging, one out-of-sample run, and a false positive rate measured on synthetic data. Whatever its Sharpe, the pipeline it exercised is the one phase 5 rebuilds properly.

title: The running strategy
text:
Portfolios and risk

Day 103 · Tue 17 Nov · The three benchmarks that beat you, and when they do not

qlib/portfolio.py starts with the three benchmark constructions. Every portfolio result for the rest of the year is reported next to them, which is the rule milestone 4 is graded on.

Day 110 · Tue 24 Nov · One covariance interface, four estimators behind it

qlib/risk.py gives the project one covariance interface with four estimators behind it, tested for positive definiteness on every window. The portfolio construction code no longer knows or cares which estimator is in use.

Day 117 · Tue 1 Dec · Neutralising a portfolio, and what it costs you

qlib/portfolio.py can now neutralise a weight vector against an arbitrary exposure set, with a test asserting the residual exposures are zero. The pairs strategy runs neutralised from here, and the unneutralised version stays as the comparison.

Day 120 · Fri 4 Dec · Targeting a volatility at the portfolio level

The book is sized to a volatility target computed from the risk model’s forecast rather than from trailing realised volatility, with an explicit leverage cap and the added turnover reported.

Day 123 · Mon 7 Dec · Backtesting a risk model: coverage and independence

qlib/risk.py can now test a risk model rather than only produce one, with coverage and independence tests that any later model has to pass before its numbers are used for sizing.

Day 130 · Mon 14 Dec · Risk of ruin, and the constraint that is not statistical

The book’s sizing now respects a hard barrier derived from maintenance margin rather than a soft statistical threshold, and qlib/portfolio.py computes the ruin probability from leverage and margin directly.

Day 131 · Tue 15 Dec · Sizing the actual book, with every number defended

The full sizing pipeline runs end to end: covariance, neutralisation, volatility target, Kelly fraction, leverage cap. Phase 6 changes only what feeds it, and phase 10 runs this exact code on a schedule.

Day 133 · Thu 17 Dec · Milestone: a factor risk model built by hand

Milestone 4 closes the portfolio phase. qlib/risk.py and qlib/portfolio.py now hold the covariance estimators, the neutralisation, the volatility target and the sizing rule, and every signal built in phase 6 flows through them unchanged.

title: The running strategy
text:
The research harness

Day 136 · Sun 20 Dec · A universe that only contains what existed at the time

The store now returns a universe as of a date, built only from information available then. Every signal from here selects from that universe, so the survivorship problem is fixed in one place rather than remembered in twelve.

Day 139 · Wed 23 Dec · The rebuild, and the test that guards it

The store’s read interface now requires an as-of date on every path and enforces per-source availability lags, with three tests that fail if a future value becomes visible. This is the foundation the event-driven engine is built on next week.

Day 142 · Sat 26 Dec · The event loop, and the order things happen in

qlib/backtest/engine.py is the event loop the rest of the year runs on. The strategy sees an as-of view rather than the store, so look-ahead is prevented by the interface rather than by care.

Day 143 · Sun 27 Dec · The fill model is where optimism hides

The engine has a pluggable fill model with three conventions and partial fills, so the price a backtest assumes is a stated configuration rather than a hidden default.

Day 144 · Mon 28 Dec · Orders have a lifecycle, and positions are derived

Fills are the primary record and everything else is derived from them, written to fills.parquet. The accounting identity is asserted at every session, which is the invariant phase 10 reconciles the live account against.

Day 145 · Tue 29 Dec · One result object, and everything downstream reads it

Every backtest now returns one serialisable result object carrying its own configuration and code version, and the tearsheet is built from that object alone. Reproducing a figure from March in July becomes a file read rather than a rerun.

Day 153 · Wed 6 Jan · The cost model, with the components separated

Costs are recorded per fill and per component in fills.parquet, so the strategy’s cost can be attributed rather than only totalled. Phase 9 replaces the impact component with a fitted one and nothing else changes.

Day 157 · Sun 10 Jan · The null strategy test, and what your engine says about nothing

The null-strategy distribution is now a characterised property of the engine and a standing test. Phase 6 evaluates every signal against this distribution rather than against zero.

Day 159 · Tue 12 Jan · One command, same number, six months later

Every result is reproducible from a configuration file and a commit hash with one command, and each result records the code version and data cutoff that produced it. This is the property that makes the platform worth showing to someone.

Day 161 · Thu 14 Jan · Milestone: the research platform

Milestone 5 closes the harness. The event loop, the fill model, the cost breakdown, the point-in-time store and the test suite are the platform every signal in phase 6 runs through, unchanged.

title: The running strategy
text:
Alpha

Day 162 · Fri 15 Jan · A signal is a forecast with a scale you have to choose

qlib/signals/base.py defines the signal interface for the whole alpha book: as-of date in, one score per security out, units declared. The two existing strategies become signals, which separates the forecast from the sizing for the first time.

Day 165 · Mon 18 Jan · Neutralise the signal, not just the portfolio

Signals are neutralised at the signal level against a standard exposure set declared once for the whole book, with the variance removed reported per signal so the cost of neutralising is visible.

Day 167 · Wed 20 Jan · The first three signals, built through the interface

Three signals are in the book, each implemented through the same interface and run through the same pipeline. Adding the fourth is now a file rather than a project, which is the property the alpha book needs.

Day 169 · Fri 22 Jan · The information coefficient is a Spearman correlation

qlib/signals/evaluate.py computes the information coefficient with a dependence-aware standard error and a null distribution from random signals, so every signal in the book is reported against a measured null rather than against zero.

Day 174 · Wed 27 Jan · One page per signal, generated rather than written

qlib/signals/report.py generates the standard one-page signal summary from the result object. Milestone 6 becomes an assembly of generated pages rather than a document that can disagree with the code.

Day 176 · Fri 29 Jan · Value, replicated with the reporting lag respected

Value joins the book as the first fundamental signal, built on the point-in-time filing schema, with the cost of getting the lag wrong measured rather than assumed.

Day 177 · Sat 30 Jan · Momentum, and the crashes that pay for its Sharpe

Momentum is in the book with its conditional crash behaviour measured and its rolling beta documented, so the sizing decision in week 29 has the tail behaviour in front of it rather than only the volatility.

Day 178 · Sun 31 Jan · Quality, and the definition problem underneath it

Six quality specifications are evaluated identically and all six are logged, so the best one is reported with the correction its selection implies rather than as a discovery.

Day 179 · Mon 1 Feb · Low volatility wins, and the explanation is a constraint

Low volatility and betting against beta are both in the book, with the leverage required by the beta-neutral construction reported explicitly, since that leverage is both the mechanism of the return and the constraint on running it.

Day 180 · Tue 2 Feb · Short-term reversal is real, and mostly a liquidity payment

Short-term reversal and size join the book. Reversal is the book’s clearest case of a signal that is real gross and dead net, and it stays in the book for exactly that reason.

Day 184 · Sat 6 Feb · Time-series momentum, and where its diversification comes from

The trend follower becomes a portfolio of trend rules across instruments and lookbacks, combined rather than selected, with the correlation structure that justifies the combination measured rather than assumed.

Day 185 · Sun 7 Feb · Carry is one definition applied to four asset classes

A carry signal built from term structure joins the book, evaluated on the same footing as everything else, with its correlation to trend measured so the combination in week 29 has a real input.

Day 190 · Fri 12 Feb · Fundamentals at scale, from EDGAR rather than a vendor

Fundamental data now comes from EDGAR directly into the store with filing dates attached, so every fundamental signal in the book is point-in-time by construction rather than by a lag applied afterwards.

Day 201 · Tue 23 Feb · The combined book, with every constraint applied

The combined alpha book runs through the whole pipeline end to end and produces one result object, with each signal’s marginal contribution computed by leave-one-out rather than by standalone performance.

Day 203 · Thu 25 Feb · Milestone: the alpha book

Milestone 6 closes the alpha phase. The book holds eight characterised signals, a measured correlation structure, a defended combination and a corrected verdict, and phase 7 asks whether a nonlinear model can beat it.

title: The running strategy
text:
Machine learning

Day 206 · Sun 28 Feb · Purging and embargoing, and why they are two fixes

qlib/ml/cv.py provides a purged and embargoed splitter with the scikit-learn interface, so every model search in the phase uses it by default and the noise experiment from day 205 is a standing test that it works.

Day 209 · Wed 3 Mar · The dataset assembly, and the test that guards it

qlib/ml/dataset.py assembles the feature matrix through the store’s as-of interface with a test that no feature value postdates its row. The poisoned-future test now covers the model path as well as the engine.

Day 212 · Sat 6 Mar · The triple barrier labels what a trade would have done

qlib/ml/labels.py implements volatility-scaled triple-barrier labelling with the outcome distribution reported, so the label reflects what a position with a stop and a target would have experienced.

Day 216 · Wed 10 Mar · Cross-sectional labels, and the demeaning that decides the bet

The modelling protocol is frozen in a committed configuration file before any model is fitted: label, horizon, weights, validation scheme and metric. Week 34’s audit compares models under it without any of them having chosen it.

Day 218 · Fri 12 Mar · The linear baseline, taken as seriously as the rival

The linear baseline is fitted and tuned under the frozen protocol with nested penalty selection, and its interval is the bar every later model in the phase is measured against.

Day 230 · Wed 24 Mar · An external scoreboard where you cannot fool yourself

A model is submitted to Numerai, which gives the year an external, live-scored track record on data where no look-ahead is available to you, alongside the internal results you produced and evaluated yourself.

Day 233 · Sat 27 Mar · The audit, run once

The audit runs once on the frozen protocol and produces the phase’s headline comparison, with every pairwise difference tested against the seed spread rather than read off a leaderboard.

Day 238 · Thu 1 Apr · Milestone: machine learning against the linear baseline

Milestone 7 closes the machine learning phase. The ML layer either joins the book with a stated marginal contribution or does not join it, and either outcome is recorded with the interval that produced the decision.

title: The running strategy
text:
Derivatives

Day 251 · Wed 14 Apr · The pricer, tested against two independent implementations

qlib/derivatives/black_scholes.py is the pricing layer for the rest of the phase, tested against an independent implementation and with implied volatility inversion that fails loudly rather than silently.

Day 278 · Tue 11 May · The variance premium as a signal, evaluated like any other

The variance risk premium signal joins the book, evaluated through the same pipeline as everything else, with an explicit note that its Sharpe ratio is not comparable to the equity signals’ because of the payoff asymmetry.

Day 280 · Thu 13 May · Milestone: an option pricer and a delta-hedging study

Milestone 8 closes the derivatives phase. qlib/derivatives holds a tested pricer, greeks, a hedging simulator and a surface fitter, and the variance risk premium signal is in the book with its asymmetry documented.

title: The running strategy
text:
Microstructure

Day 292 · Tue 25 May · The square-root law, tested on your own data

The impact exponent and coefficient in qlib/costs.py are replaced by values fitted to real data with a stated uncertainty, which retires the largest assumption in every cost and capacity number reported since week 22.

Day 296 · Sat 29 May · The efficient frontier of execution, and where to sit on it

qlib/exec/schedule.py generates an execution trajectory from an order, a horizon and a stated risk aversion, using the fitted impact model rather than the linear assumption in the original paper.

Day 298 · Mon 31 May · Implementation shortfall counts the trade you missed

qlib/exec/shortfall.py measures implementation shortfall with opportunity cost included and its components reconciling to the total, which becomes the standard execution metric for the paper account in phase 10.

Day 299 · Tue 1 Jun · Measuring your own slippage, against your own decisions

The engine records decision, submission and fill timestamps with the prevailing mid at each, so implementation shortfall is measurable on the paper account from today rather than reconstructed later.

Day 302 · Fri 4 Jun · Capacity, recomputed with a fitted model

Every capacity figure in the alpha book is recomputed from the fitted impact model, and the combined book’s capacity accounts for signals competing for the same liquidity rather than being the sum of the parts.

Day 303 · Sat 5 Jun · Which strategy dies first as the money grows

The book is re-optimised at ten and a hundred times current size with size-dependent costs, showing how the composition changes as capacity binds rather than only how performance falls.

Day 308 · Thu 10 Jun · Milestone: execution, impact and honest capacity

Milestone 9 closes the microstructure phase. The cost model’s impact term is now fitted rather than assumed, every capacity figure has been revised, and the engine records what it needs to measure the live account’s shortfall in phase 10.

title: The running strategy
text:
Production

Day 323 · Fri 25 Jun · The daily run, as a sequence of steps that can each fail

qlib/run/daily.py is the production entry point: seven ordered steps, each with an explicit success condition, and three checks for the failures that do not raise exceptions.

Day 324 · Sat 26 Jun · Logging for the questions you will ask in March

The production run emits structured JSON logs with run identifiers, per-step timings and the numbers behind each decision, so any day’s positions can be reconstructed from the log without rerunning the pipeline.

Day 325 · Sun 27 Jun · Monitoring the four things that actually break

Four monitors with thresholds calibrated against historical data run alongside the daily pipeline, each reporting a number rather than a boolean so that near-misses are visible before they become failures.

Day 326 · Mon 28 Jun · Alerting, and the runbook written before you need it

Alerts are routed by severity and every one has a runbook entry with ranked causes, diagnostic commands and a safe action, written before the first real incident rather than after it.

Day 327 · Tue 29 Jun · Reconciliation, and explaining every difference

Daily reconciliation compares intended against actual positions and cash with every difference attributed to a named cause, and an unexplained residual raises an alert rather than being absorbed.

Day 328 · Wed 30 Jun · The first unattended run, and what it got wrong

The pipeline runs unattended on a schedule, and the first failure is diagnosed from logs alone and fixed, with the failure category recorded in the runbook.

Day 329 · Thu 1 Jul · Milestone: the system in production

Milestone 10 closes the production phase. The book runs on a schedule against a paper account with monitoring, reconciliation and a runbook, and the track record it produces from here is the one the capstone reports without adjustment.

title: The running strategy
text:
The interview

Day 352 · Sat 24 Jul · Three write-ups a stranger can read in ten minutes

The three write-ups are the form in which the year’s work actually gets read: result first, one figure, interval, specification count, and the most serious limitation, each in two pages.

Day 357 · Thu 29 Jul · Milestone: the interview dossier

Milestone 11 assembles the year’s work into the form a hiring process consumes: three two-page write-ups drawn from the milestones, a CV that describes the genetics work in the language of the job, and a firm list with outreach already sent.

title: The running strategy
text:
Capstone

Day 358 · Fri 30 Jul · The track record, reported without adjustment

The live paper track record is reported with every period included and reconciled against the broker’s own statements, with the Sharpe standard error at this sample length stated on the same page as the estimate.

Day 359 · Sat 31 Jul · Where the live period disagreed with the backtest

The live-against-backtest difference is decomposed into execution, universe and signal components that sum to the total, which is the first empirical test of the ranked list of lies from milestone 5.

Day 360 · Sun 1 Aug · The research dossier, assembled from eleven documents

The research dossier pulls the year into one document with every claim traced to a milestone and a configuration, verified by reproducing three claims at random from a clean checkout.

Day 361 · Mon 2 Aug · What you would actually run, and at what size

The dossier gains a recommendation section: which components to run, at what capital and Kelly fraction, with the expected interval and accepted drawdown, and an explicit list of what is excluded and why.

Day 365 · Fri 6 Aug · Capstone

The system that started as an empty DuckDB file on day 20 now ingests, forecasts, sizes, executes, reconciles and reports on a schedule, with a track record it did not tamper with and a written account of everything it still gets wrong.

title: Setup
text: Nothing here is hard. It is here so that no day in the next year begins with an install.

title: Setup
text:
The environment
You already have uv from the LLM bootcamp. A separate environment, because the two courses pin different things and you do not want a PyTorch upgrade to break a backtest in March.
uv venv ~/.venvs/quant --python 3.12
source ~/.venvs/quant/bin/activate
Then the core stack. This is the whole list for weeks 1 through 20; the derivatives and C++ tooling arrives when you need it, in phase 8 and phase 10.
uv pip install --python ~/.venvs/quant/bin/python \
  numpy pandas polars pyarrow duckdb scipy statsmodels scikit-learn \
  matplotlib seaborn jupyterlab \
  arch linearmodels cvxpy \
  yfinance pandas-datareader requests \
  pytest ruff
What each of those is for, so that none of it is cargo cult:







Package
Why it is in the list




duckdb + pyarrow
Your data store. SQL directly over Parquet files, no server. It doubles as the place you learn SQL properly in week 45.


polars
For anything large or repeated. Keep pandas too — most quant code you will ever read is pandas.


statsmodels
Time series, state space and the Kalman filter. statsmodels.tsa and statsmodels.statespace are weeks 10–14.


arch
Kevin Sheppard’s package. GARCH, unit-root tests, the bootstrap, and the Reality Check / SPA tests you need in week 8.


linearmodels
Also Sheppard’s. Panel models, IV/2SLS and Fama-MacBeth regressions. The IV code will look familiar.


cvxpy
Convex optimization. Phase 4 writes portfolio constraints by hand rather than calling a black box.


yfinance
Free daily bars, good enough to learn on. It is unofficial and personal-use only — week 3 covers what it gets wrong and what replaces it.

title: Setup
text:
Accounts
Five minutes each, and every one is free. Do these tonight because two of them take a day to approve.

Alpaca — free paper trading and a market-data API. This is the broker the running strategy eventually trades against. Sign up now; the account is used from week 3 and seriously from week 47.
Nasdaq Data Link — free API key, used for some of the reference datasets.
Kaggle — several past competitions (Optiver realized volatility, Jane Street market prediction) released real data that phases 6 and 7 use as a proving ground.
Numerai — a free tournament on obfuscated financial data with real payouts. You will submit to it from phase 7, and it is the one public track record that quant employers actually recognise.
Interactive Brokers — optional and slower to open. Their paper account is the more realistic execution environment if you want it in phase 10.

You do not need a Bloomberg terminal, a paid data subscription, or a broker with real money in it. Not this year.






Check whether UW-Madison licenses WRDS. If it does, you get CRSP and Compustat — survivorship-free US equity history with point-in-time fundamentals, which is the single largest data-quality upgrade available to you and costs an institution tens of thousands of dollars a year. Ask the business school library. Week 3 assumes free data and tells you what it is missing; if WRDS comes through, that week gets much better.

title: Setup
text:
Two repositories
Same split that worked for the LLM bootcamp: the plan is one repo, the work is another.
projects/
├── quant-365-day-bootcamp/    this site, and data/schedule.yml
└── quant-365-work/            your notebooks, code and reports  ← work here
Create the work repo now, private, and give it this shape:
quant-365-work/
├── env.sh                  activates ~/.venvs/quant and sets QUANT_DATA
├── data/                   gitignored — parquet, duckdb files, downloads
├── notebooks/              one per day, named by day number
├── qlib/                   the package you actually build: ingest, signals, backtest, exec
├── reports/                the twelve milestone documents
└── tests/
Name notebooks by day — notebooks/day-047-sharpe-standard-error.ipynb — because on day 203 a milestone report needs a result from week 7 and you will not remember which week it was.
Gitignore the data. Commit the query, the date range, the universe definition and the seed. Never the Parquet files. You already work this way with genotype data; the reasoning is identical and the file sizes are smaller.

title: Setup
section: What a year of data actually costs you in disk
text:
What a year of data actually costs you in disk
Plan for this now so week 3 does not surprise you.







What
Roughly




Daily bars, ~5,000 US equities and ETFs, 20 years
2–4 GB as Parquet


Minute bars, ~500 names, 5 years
40–80 GB


One month of full order book for one liquid crypto pair
20–60 GB


Ken French factor returns, FRED series, everything in phase 2
under 100 MB



Phases 1 through 8 fit comfortably in the first row. Only phase 9 needs the third, and only for a few symbols and a few days.

title: Setup
text:
Verify
If this prints a table of returns and a Sharpe ratio, you are ready for day 1.
import duckdb, yfinance as yf, numpy as np

px = yf.download("SPY", start="2015-01-01", end="2025-01-01", auto_adjust=True)["Close"]
r = np.log(px / px.shift(1)).dropna()

print(f"{len(r)} daily observations, {r.index[0].date()} to {r.index[-1].date()}")
print(f"annualised mean  {r.mean() * 252:.3f}")
print(f"annualised vol   {r.std() * np.sqrt(252):.3f}")
print(f"Sharpe (rf = 0)  {r.mean() / r.std() * np.sqrt(252):.3f}")
print(duckdb.sql("select 42 as duckdb_works").fetchall())
Three things about that snippet are wrong or misleading, and you will be able to name all three by day 50. auto_adjust=True is doing something to the price history that week 3 makes you look at. The Sharpe ratio has no standard error attached, which week 7 fixes. And rf = 0 was defensible in 2021 and is not now. Leave the code as it is; it is a marker.

title: Setup
section: Where the year’s reading comes from
text:
Where the year’s reading comes from
Most of the resources are free — MIT OpenCourseWare, QuantEcon, Ken French’s data library, arXiv, and the free lecture notes from Oxford, Princeton and NYU. Some are not, and the paid ones are concentrated in two places:

Phase 8 (derivatives) leans on Shreve and on Hull. Free lecture notes cover most of it, and the day pages name them, but if you buy one book for this year, buy Shreve volume II.
Phase 11 (the interview) leans on the Green Book and Heard on the Street. There is no free substitute of comparable quality, they are cheap, and you will use them for fifty drill sittings.

Everything else has a free path. Where a day depends on a paid book, it names a free alternative in the same resource list.

title: Setup
text:
One honest warning before day 1
You are about to spend 365 hours on a field that is unusually good at producing convincing-looking results that are not real. The single most valuable thing you bring is the instinct that a striking result is probably a multiple-testing artifact until shown otherwise — you have that instinct because genome-wide association studies had their own reckoning with it a decade before you arrived.
Keep it. Phases 2 and 5 exist to make it quantitative, and by phase 6 it will be the thing that distinguishes your research from most of what gets published in this field.
